title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
authors: Andi Gu, Alek H. Kemeny, Susanne F. Yelin, Mikhail D. Lukin
abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

infographic.key_insight: An evaluator-guided LLM search can discover quantum circuits and reversible architectures that improve state-of-the-art resource efficiency across multiple problem classes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work suggests a practical design loop for reducing Toffoli gates and qubit counts in quantum algorithms, which directly matters for near-term resource-constrained quantum hardware.
method: LLMs propose candidate quantum circuit designs.
An independent evaluator verifies and scores each design.
Evolutionary search iterates over tasks in computation, chemistry, optimization, simulation, and number theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight tasks, seven showed significant reductions in both Toffoli and qubit counts versus prior art, and the eighth produced a new reversible modular inversion architecture.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on the quality of the evaluator and search space, so gains may not transfer uniformly to all quantum algorithms or hardware constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models

title: Post-Optimization Subspace Corrections to Quantum Ansätze
authors: Prince Frederick Kwao, Bharath Sambasivam, Jason Saroni, Srivathsan Poyyapakkam Sundar, Edwin Barnes, Ayush Asthana
abstract: Circuit depth and measurement count are the main limitations for chemical applications of the leading variational quantum algorithms on quantum computers. We show that both resource requirements can be reduced by augmenting adaptive variational quantum algorithms with post-optimization corrective techniques. We focus on two such techniques---Hamiltonian-moment Krylov subspace diagonalization and the identity-augmented quantum self-consistent equation of motion (q-sc-EOM)---applied to optimized ADAPT-VQE states without further ansatz growth or nonlinear optimization. Across molecular systems studied with up to 20 qubits, first-order Krylov correction reduces the optimized iterations (and the corresponding number of adaptive layers) needed to reach the $1.6~\mathrm{m}E_h$ threshold by up to approximately sixfold, with a general trend toward larger reductions at higher determinant Rényi entropy. We also find measurement-cost reductions of up to approximately fortyfold using a suitable resource-cost model. Identity-augmented q-sc-EOM improves molecular potential-energy curves obtained from truncated ADAPT-VQE ansätze with limited expressivity and recovers accuracy from states produced by sampled operator ranking without additional gradient-based operator selection, providing an advantage when small pool gradients make selection measurement intensive. Together, these post-optimization corrections offer routes to improve energy accuracy and reduce adaptive circuit growth in quantum algorithms as quantum hardware advances.

infographic.key_insight: Post-optimization corrections can substantially improve ADAPT-VQE results without adding new ansatz layers or running another nonlinear optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These methods reduce both circuit depth and measurement cost, making chemically relevant quantum simulations more practical on near-term hardware.
method: Hamiltonian-moment Krylov subspace diagonalization is applied after ADAPT-VQE optimization to refine energies.
Identity-augmented q-sc-EOM corrects truncated or sampled ADAPT-VQE states to recover accuracy.
Both approaches act as post-processing steps, so they avoid further ansatz growth.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across molecular systems up to 20 qubits, first-order Krylov correction reduced the iterations needed to reach the 1.6 mE_h threshold by up to about 6× and reduced measurement cost by up to about 40×.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on state quality and cost-model assumptions, so gains may be smaller when gradients are noisy or the underlying ansatz is extremely limited.
infographic.paper_title: Post-Optimization Subspace Corrections to Quantum Ansätze

title: Jianmu-Q: Bridging Quantum Field Theory and Quantum Hardware with AI Agents
authors: Xiaolin Wang, Xingyu Guo, Jinyang Li, Tianyin Li, Enke Wang, Lingxiao Wang
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to non-perturbative simulations of quantum field theories, particularly for real-time dynamics and systems affected by the sign problem. Yet translating continuum field theories into quantum computations remains a challenging interdisciplinary task. Here we introduce \texttt{Jianmu-Q}, a multi-agent framework that transforms natural-language descriptions of quantum field theories into quantum simulation workflows. Specialized agents handle theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design, while physical consistency checks and independent numerical calculations provide validation throughout the workflow. We benchmark the framework on three field theories of increasing complexity: the $(1+1)$-dimensional Nambu--Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models, and a $(2+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory. Across these systems, noiseless quantum-circuit simulations converge toward independent exact-diagonalization and tensor-network results, while selected circuits are executed on IBM quantum hardware, demonstrating an end-to-end, validation-guided approach to quantum simulation of field theories.

infographic.key_insight: Jianmu-Q uses coordinated AI agents to convert natural-language quantum field theory descriptions into validated quantum simulation workflows spanning theory, discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework lowers the translation burden between continuum field theory and quantum hardware, enabling more reproducible end-to-end quantum software pipelines for scientific computing.
method: Specialized agents handle theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit synthesis.
Physical-consistency checks and independent numerical calculations validate each stage of the workflow.
Benchmarked on the (1+1)D Nambu--Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models plus a (2+1)D Z2 gauge theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three benchmark field theories, noiseless circuit simulations matched independent exact-diagonalization and tensor-network results, and selected circuits were run on IBM hardware.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on accurate agent coordination and validation, and hardware runs remain constrained by present-day quantum device noise and scale limits.
infographic.paper_title: Jianmu-Q: Bridging Quantum Field Theory and Quantum Hardware with AI Agents

title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
authors: João Santos, Jayshankar Nath, Marco Pezzutto, Valentin Savin, Tristan Meunier, Yasser Omar
abstract: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that spin-qubit quantum computers can become energetically competitive with classical computing before they achieve an execution-time advantage, especially when energy is measured for QFT workloads and then extended to fault-tolerant operation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scalable quantum hardware design, the dominant constraints are cryogenic cooling, control electronics, and decoding overheads, making energy-efficient system architecture as important as qubit performance.
method: Built a detailed energy budget for a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit computer running the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT).
Benchmarked QFT energy use against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) under polynomially bounded sampling assumptions.
Extended the analysis to surface-code QEC, including QEC cycles, gate synthesis, decoding, and control-signal demultiplexing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that optimized demultiplexing can cut total energy by roughly two orders of magnitude and estimates about 100 kW power for a system with around one million physical qubits.
infographic.watch_item: The power estimates depend strongly on cryogenic and control-stack assumptions, so real hardware implementations may shift the crossover points and total energy cost.
infographic.paper_title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation

title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs
authors: L. Sunil Chandran, Rishikesh Gajjala
abstract: Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was known. We prove that every simple connected GHZ graph $G$ with at least four vertices has dimension at most $2^{κ(G)-1}+\binom{κ(G)}{2}$, where $κ(G)$ is the vertex connectivity of $G$. We also prove new bounds in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proves a new upper bound on the dimension of simple connected GHZ graphs in terms of vertex connectivity: at most 2^(κ(G)-1) + C(κ(G),2).
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives quantum optics and distributed quantum computing a graph-theoretic limit on how large a GHZ state can be generated from a given connectivity structure.
method: Translate GHZ photonic experiments into edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs.
Bound the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings using graph connectivity parameters.
Derive additional bounds using edge connectivity and maximum degree.
infographic.evidence_signal: The result is theoretical and extends prior proofs for graphs with vertex connectivity at most 2, tightening the known limits from the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: The bound is only for simple connected GHZ graphs, so it may not directly cover more general experimental graph constructions or weighted/irregular variants.
infographic.paper_title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs

title: Magic in quantum trajectory unravelings of noisy random quantum circuits
authors: Sara Santos, Alessio Paviglianiti, Vincenzo Savona
abstract: The quantum-trajectory description of a noisy quantum circuit is not unique: every Kraus representation of the noise channel defines a different unraveling, i.e., a different ensemble of pure states that averages to the same density matrix. While all unravelings share the same expectation values of observables, they generally differ in the amount of quantum resources carried by the individual trajectories. Here we study non-stabilizerness, or magic, quantified by the stabilizer Rényi entropy, in quantum-trajectory unravelings of Haar-random and $T$-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits subject to local dephasing noise of strength $p$. The canonical unraveling in terms of Pauli jumps is Clifford and leaves magic untouched, so that trajectories retain the Haar-random value of non-stabilizerness. Exploring the full two-parameter family of minimal unravelings, we find that the trajectory-averaged magic can be substantially reduced by a state-independent choice of Kraus operators, and that the optimal choice is not in general the projective-measurement unraveling, but a two-outcome generalized measurement in which the Kraus operators correspond to a weak measurement of the noisy qubit. The optimal unraveling reduces the extensive magic density of the trajectories by a $p$-dependent factor without altering its linear scaling with system size. At the same time, it produces a very broad distribution of magic over trajectories, with a sizable fraction of trajectories retaining Haar-random magic. Since the cost of stabilizer-based classical simulation grows exponentially with the magic of the state, these high-magic trajectories, rather than the average, control the simulation cost. Our results delineate the potential and the limitations of unraveling optimization as a route to the classical simulation of noisy quantum dynamics with stabilizer methods.

infographic.key_insight: Optimizing the noise unraveling can lower the average trajectory magic in noisy random circuits, but a broad tail of high-magic trajectories still remains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For stabilizer-based simulation, the worst-case/high-magic trajectories—not the mean—set the practical computational cost, so unraveling choice matters for algorithm design.
method: Analyzed Haar-random and T-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits under local dephasing noise.
Compared the canonical Pauli-jump unraveling against the full family of minimal Kraus unravelings.
Identified an optimal two-outcome weak-measurement unraveling that minimizes trajectory-averaged stabilizer Rényi entropy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the optimal unraveling reduces extensive magic density by a p-dependent factor while preserving linear scaling with system size, but leaves a sizable fraction of trajectories near Haar-random magic.
infographic.watch_item: Magic is highly broad-distributed across trajectories, so optimizing the mean does not guarantee a large reduction in classical simulation cost.
infographic.paper_title: Magic in quantum trajectory unravelings of noisy random quantum circuits

title: Agent-assisted experimental strategy transfer across quantum processors
authors: Shi-Yao Hou, Zipeng Wu, Chao Zhang, Guanru Feng, Keren Li, Jingen Xiang
abstract: Progress in quantum hardware requires a growing volume of experiments across diverse devices, straining the capacity of human experts. Automation remains challenging because device differences and drift can render workflows developed on one processor unsuitable for another. Here we present an agent-assisted experimental strategy for conducting experiments across three-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance processors. Developed on one processor and applied sequentially to four others, the strategy uses an agent to assess experimental evidence, select subsequent measurements and adapt procedures, with operators providing instrument preparation and physical intervention. Using three-qubit Grover state preparation as a common task, each deployment combined device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization and measurement. The experimental strategy was refined through sequential deployment, and all four processors ultimately produced outputs dominated by their respective marked states. The marked-state populations of the reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranged from \(0.910\) to \(0.959\), with relative deviations below \(3.8\%\) from the ideal value of 0.945. These results demonstrate that an agent-assisted experimental strategy can be reused and refined across processors to realize a common quantum task, providing a basis for scaling experimental practice beyond individual devices.

infographic.key_insight: An agent-guided experimental workflow can be transferred and refined across different quantum processors to reliably execute the same quantum task despite hardware differences and drift.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a practical route to scale quantum experimentation beyond hand-tuned, device-specific procedures by combining automated decision-making with human operator intervention.
method: Developed the strategy on one three-qubit NMR processor and deployed it sequentially on four others.
Used an agent to evaluate evidence, choose the next measurements, and adapt procedures.
Combined device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization, and measurement for three-qubit Grover state preparation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four processors, the reconstructed dominant eigenstates had marked-state populations from 0.910 to 0.959, with relative deviations below 3.8% from the ideal 0.945.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on operator-side instrument preparation and physical intervention, so full autonomy and broader hardware transferability remain limited.
infographic.paper_title: Agent-assisted experimental strategy transfer across quantum processors

title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
authors: Nicholas S. DiBrita, Jack Lange, Tirthak Patel
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

infographic.key_insight: SynDebug is a systems-level debugging framework that brings lightweight assertion-based checks directly into fault-tolerant quantum computing programs without materially increasing logical error risk.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical way to debug realistic encoded FTQC workflows, helping engineers validate complex quantum software beyond idealized logical circuits.
method: Adds assertion-based debugging primitives inside encoded FTQC execution flows
Avoids extra logical surface area while keeping temporal overhead low
Supports multiple QEC code families, code distances, and workloads
infographic.evidence_signal: Across state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs, SynDebug averaged 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead, was 0% in most cases, and showed no measurable increase in logical error rate.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is lightweight, but real deployment still depends on careful integration with specific QEC stacks and workload-specific assertion placement.
infographic.paper_title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs

title: Quantum control of solid state qubits via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Dennis Herb, Mirko Rossini, Sabine Wölk, Joachim Ankerhold, Dominik Maile, Alessio Belenchia
abstract: The use of reinforcement learning (RL) in the design of quantum control strategies for pulse level control of NISQ era quantum devices is attracting growing interest. Model-free RL, not requiring preexisting knowledge of the physical system, acts as a black-box optimization tool well suited for noisy devices. In this work, we provide a simulation-based analysis of the performance of model-free RL for state preparation and qubit gate design in a challenging setup: indirect control of NV nuclear spins in a spin-bath. In particular, the spin-bath is modeled via the generalized cluster correlation expansion accounting for magnetic impurities and intra-bath interactions. We analyze the performance of the RL agents by performing simulations with minimally observable environments and noisy, sparse rewards as introduced in (Phys. Rev. X 12, 011059), and compare them to other state-of-the-art black-box optimization tools.

infographic.key_insight: Model-free reinforcement learning can optimize pulse-level quantum control for difficult solid-state qubits even when the system dynamics are only weakly observed and noisy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a practical black-box route for state preparation and gate design in NISQ hardware where accurate system models are unavailable or costly to build.
method: Simulated indirect control of NV nuclear spins embedded in a spin-bath.
Used a generalized cluster correlation expansion to model magnetic impurities and intra-bath interactions.
Evaluated RL agents under minimally observable environments with noisy, sparse rewards and compared them to other black-box optimizers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports a simulation-based performance analysis for state preparation and qubit gate design, benchmarking RL against other state-of-the-art black-box optimization methods.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated in simulation, so real hardware deployment may face additional sensitivity to calibration drift, measurement noise, and reward sparsity.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum control of solid state qubits via Reinforcement Learning

title: Same Spectrum, Harder First-Order Training: Phase-Locking in Single- versus Multi-Qubit Re-Uploading Circuits
authors: Michael Poppel, David Bucher, Maximilian Zorn, Markus Baumann, Sebastian Wölckert, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien
abstract: Angle-encoded variational quantum circuits implement truncated Fourier series. For one-dimensional inputs, a single-qubit re-uploading (serial) circuit represents every function that a multi-qubit circuit with the same encoding budget $E$ can; we find that this exchange of width for depth is not free in first-order training. Because its state lives on the Bloch sphere, all parameters of the serial circuit move the state, at each input, along one complex direction, which we call \emph{phase-locking}. We prove that this costs no Fourier direction but leaves no direction to spare: however many parameters it has, the serial circuit has at most $2E+2$ tangent directions, one more than its $2E+1$ Fourier coefficients need, while a two-qubit control with the same encoding budget and model class generically has at least $6E+6$. The cost in training is measured against this control, as the number of runs out of 100 that reach the optimum within a fixed step budget. On an exact loss with flat-spectrum targets the gap grows with $E$; at $E=32$ the serial circuit converges in 3, 53 and 83 runs under gradient descent, Adam and Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in 99, 100 and 100. On three real-world series, at matched parameter counts, the serial circuit reaches the least-squares optimum in at most 9 runs under Adam and in 32 to 93 under Levenberg--Marquardt, the control in at least 98 and in all 100; its held-out error is up to about $1.5$ times that of the control under Adam, but no larger in the typical run under Levenberg--Marquardt.

infographic.key_insight: Single-qubit re-uploading circuits can match the expressivity of multi-qubit circuits with the same encoding budget, but their first-order training is much harder because all parameters become phase-locked on the Bloch sphere.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum machine learning, increasing circuit depth instead of width can preserve function class while sharply degrading optimization reliability, so architecture choice must consider trainability as well as expressivity.
method: Analyzed Fourier-series expressivity of angle-encoded variational circuits with encoding budget E.
Proved the serial single-qubit circuit has at most 2E+2 tangent directions, while a comparable two-qubit control generically has at least 6E+6.
Benchmarked gradient descent, Adam, and Levenberg–Marquardt on exact flat-spectrum targets and three real-world time series.
infographic.evidence_signal: At E=32 on the exact loss, the serial circuit converged in 3/53/83 runs under gradient descent/Adam/Levenberg–Marquardt, versus 99/100/100 for the two-qubit control; on real data it also showed worse or only matched held-out error depending on optimizer.
infographic.watch_item: The advantage of the wider control model is demonstrated under matched encoding budget and parameter-count settings, so results may depend on optimizer choice, initialization, and the specific one-dimensional encoding regime.
infographic.paper_title: Same Spectrum, Harder First-Order Training: Phase-Locking in Single- versus Multi-Qubit Re-Uploading Circuits

title: Efficient quantum simulation of unitary gates based on atomic ensembles
authors: Manish Chaudhary, Tim Byrnes
abstract: We develop a technique to perform efficient unitary time evolution of a general spin Hamiltonian based on the system with identical qubits, as naturally realized by permutation symmetric atomic ensembles. We employ Cartan decomposition method to the associated Hamiltonian Lie algebra and construct the symmetry adapted generators to implement unitary operator of the ensemble Hamiltonian. This enables the compact circuit representations of the system dynamics in terms of experimentally accessible collective spin operations and exploits the Dicke basis structure of the ensembles as an effective qudit representation. We benchmark Cartan based evolution against both exact time evolution and the Suzuki Trotter product formula. Our results show that the Cartan protocol accurately reproduces the operator dynamics, spin expectation values, and fluctuation observables with zero error that are substantially smaller than those obtained through Trotterization while maintaining an optimized circuit structure. In addition, scaling analysis with the ensemble size demonstrates that the Cartan error remains independent of the atom number while the corresponding Trotter error increases with the system size, highlighting the improved efficiency of the Cartan approach for a larger system size.

infographic.key_insight: Cartan-decomposition-based simulation lets permutation-symmetric atomic ensembles implement general unitary spin dynamics efficiently using collective spin operations and the Dicke basis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach reduces circuit complexity and improves scaling for simulating many-qubit symmetric quantum systems, making it attractive for larger ensemble-based quantum hardware.
method: Use Cartan decomposition on the Hamiltonian Lie algebra to build symmetry-adapted generators.
Represent the ensemble in the Dicke basis as an effective qudit system.
Implement dynamics with compact collective-spin circuits and compare against exact evolution and Suzuki-Trotterization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the Cartan protocol matches exact dynamics with zero error and consistently outperforms Trotterization, with error staying independent of atom number while Trotter error grows with system size.
infographic.watch_item: The method is tailored to permutation-symmetric ensemble Hamiltonians, so performance may be limited when symmetry is broken or the target system is not collective-spin friendly.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient quantum simulation of unitary gates based on atomic ensembles

title: ZZ-Free bSWAP Gates under Strong Driving in Far-Detuned Fixed-Frequency Transmons
authors: Akinori Machino, Kazuhisa Ogawa, Yuto Ikegai, Takafumi Miyanaga, Koichiro Ban, Nilton F. G. Filho
abstract: Far-detuned frequency allocations in fixed-frequency superconducting processors mitigate spectral crowding but constrain cross-resonance interactions at practical drive amplitudes. Here, we demonstrate that a single strong drive induces a large $XX-YY$ interaction in the far-detuned regime, while a weak second tone tunes the accompanying $ZZ$ phase. The interaction realizes a 150-ns $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gate, which can directly prepare a maximally entangled state from the ground state. For the implementations on the same qubit pair at matched drive strengths, cross resonance gives a shorter CNOT operation, while $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gives a 33% shorter SWAP operation with a higher IRB fidelity. The multilevel theory further predicts a regime where stronger driving can yield a speed advantage for CNOT as well, a possibility absent in the two-level model. As an application of the $XX-YY$ interaction, we also demonstrate two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit through two-axis countertwisting. The interaction realized here complements cross resonance and offers a route to efficient gate synthesis and quantum simulation of interacting spin systems.

infographic.key_insight: A strong drive on far-detuned fixed-frequency transmons can generate a large XX-YY interaction, enabling a fast ZZ-free bSWAP gate with tunable phase control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides an alternative to cross-resonance for gate synthesis, with better SWAP efficiency and a path to improved two-qubit operations in spectrally crowded superconducting processors.
method: Apply a single strong drive to induce the XX-YY coupling in the far-detuned regime.
Use a weak second tone to compensate and tune away the unwanted ZZ interaction.
Demonstrate a 150-ns sqrt(bSWAP) gate and two-spin squeezing via two-axis countertwisting.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports direct experimental implementation and comparison on the same qubit pair, showing faster SWAP and higher IRB fidelity for sqrt(bSWAP), plus a multilevel-theory prediction of a stronger-drive CNOT advantage.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on careful multi-tone calibration and strong-driving conditions, so performance may depend sensitively on device-specific multilevel dynamics and drive-induced errors.
infographic.paper_title: ZZ-Free bSWAP Gates under Strong Driving in Far-Detuned Fixed-Frequency Transmons

title: A modular quantum computer based on Cornucopia codes
authors: Zhide Lu, Weikang Li, Yinghao Ma, Hanyu Yan, Bingrun Wang, Yixuan Ma
abstract: Ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes store many logical qubits in a single code block with few physical qubits. A fault-tolerant quantum computer, however, also requires a universal set of logical operations on individually addressable logical qubits, and the ancilla overhead of these operations may erode the advantage of the high encoding rate. Here, we propose the Cornucopia architecture, in which a universal set of logical operations is implemented at low overhead for the Cornucopia codes. In particular, we focus on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code as an example and introduce a modular quantum computer built from such code blocks connected by bridges. Each block stores 1,426 logical qubits and serves as a universal logical processor. Exploiting the code's translation symmetry, we construct a family of reusable gadgets that individually address 1,422 logical qubits within each block. These gadgets support three universal logical instruction sets: basic, high-throughput and fixed-extractor. Excluding magic-state factories, a module with sufficient workspace to execute any instruction in the basic set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with 3.0 for memory alone. The architecture thus preserves the resource advantage of ultra-high-rate quantum memory while enabling universal logical computation, providing a route towards low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computers.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that Cornucopia ultra-high-rate quantum codes can be turned into a modular architecture that supports universal logical computation with low overhead.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters because it preserves the memory efficiency of high-rate error correction while adding practical, individually addressable logical operations needed for fault-tolerant quantum computers.
method: Use the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code as the core block, storing 1,426 logical qubits per module.
Connect blocks with bridges to form a modular quantum computer.
Exploit translation symmetry to build reusable gadgets that address 1,422 logical qubits and support basic, high-throughput, and fixed-extractor instruction sets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that a module capable of running any basic instruction set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, versus 3.0 for memory alone.
infographic.watch_item: The architecture’s advantage depends on available workspace and excludes magic-state factories, so full system overhead may be higher in practice.
infographic.paper_title: A modular quantum computer based on Cornucopia codes

title: Deterministic and programmable generation of mechanical multipartite entangled states
authors: Isabelle Franzen, Max-Emanuel Kern, Q. Rumman Rahman, Igor Kladarić, Stefano Marti, Yiwen Chu
abstract: Multimode mechanical resonators offer a large set of densely packed, long-lived bosonic modes within a single compact device, making them attractive for quantum simulation, quantum information processing, and quantum-enhanced sensing. Many such applications rely on multipartite entanglement, yet deterministic mechanical entanglement has so far been largely limited to pairs of modes. Here we demonstrate the deterministic and programmable preparation of multipartite entangled states among the phonon modes of a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator coupled to a superconducting transmon qubit. By sequentially applying optimal-control-engineered isometries between the qubit and successive modes, we generate matrix product states of bond dimension two, including $W$, Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ), and cluster states. We fully characterize these states via quantum state tomography and certify genuine multipartite entanglement among up to four modes. We further demonstrate correlated-noise sensing by exploiting the complementary decoherence responses of the stored $W$ and GHZ states, isolating inter-mode phase correlations from local decoherence and placing quantitative bounds on collective dephasing. Our results establish a scalable approach to preparing multipartite entangled states in mechanical systems, with promising applications in multiparameter sensing and tests of quantum mechanics with massive objects.

infographic.key_insight: A superconducting transmon qubit can deterministically and programmatically generate multipartite entangled mechanical states across multiple phonon modes, including W, GHZ, and cluster states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a scalable control strategy for compact multimode mechanical platforms that could enable quantum simulation, sensing, and information storage on chip.
method: Sequentially apply optimal-control-engineered isometries between the qubit and selected mechanical modes.
Prepare matrix product states with bond dimension two in a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator.
Use quantum state tomography to certify the generated entangled states and probe correlated-noise sensing behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports full characterization by tomography, genuine multipartite entanglement certification across up to four modes, and quantitative bounds on collective dephasing from W/GHZ decoherence comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability will depend on maintaining high-fidelity qubit-mode control and managing decoherence as the number of mechanical modes increases.
infographic.paper_title: Deterministic and programmable generation of mechanical multipartite entangled states

title: Dynamical Decoupling of Nonclassical States in a Biased-Noise Spin Qudit
authors: Arjen Vaartjes, Namit Anand, Rocky Y. Su, Akram Youssry, Ritik Sareen, Jeffrey Marshall
abstract: Encoding quantum information in $d$-dimensional systems (qudits) with $d>2$ offers appealing new directions for resource-efficient quantum computing. However, protecting the coherence of nonclassical qudit resource states remains an open challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a well-established technique for extending coherence, but its application to qudits is hindered by the quadratic scaling of the decoupling sequence overhead with the dimension $d$. As a result, demonstrations of qudit DD have so far been limited to low-dimensional qudits. Here, we show that noise-biased qudits enable a nontrivial reduction of this overhead, for example, from quadratic to linear. We perform qudit DD on a model $d=8$ qudit, the nuclear spin of an antimony donor in silicon. We benchmark DD performance on highly nonclassical states such as uniform superpositions, cat states, and Haar random states and measure coherence improvements up to a factor $5$ to $10$. For a spin-cat error correction code, continuous DD extends the coherence time of the logical superposition $|+\rangle_L$ to $225$~ms, compared to $19$~ms under free evolution and $85$~ms with a Hahn echo. This improvement shows that DD sequences tailored to a system's noise bias can significantly enhance the lifetime of encoded logical qubits.

infographic.key_insight: Noise-biased qudits can make dynamical decoupling far more efficient, cutting the pulse overhead from quadratic to roughly linear in dimension while significantly extending coherence of nonclassical states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical path to longer-lived logical qubits in higher-dimensional spin systems, improving the viability of resource-efficient quantum computing hardware.
method: Implemented dynamical decoupling on a model d=8 qudit: an antimony donor nuclear spin in silicon.
Exploited biased noise to reduce sequence overhead compared with standard qudit DD.
Benchmarked performance on uniform superpositions, cat states, Haar-random states, and a spin-cat code.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports coherence improvements of about 5–10×, with the logical |+>_L coherence extended to 225 ms versus 19 ms for free evolution and 85 ms for Hahn echo.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on strong noise bias and system-specific pulse design, so performance may not transfer directly to all qudit platforms.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamical Decoupling of Nonclassical States in a Biased-Noise Spin Qudit

title: The Generalized BEADS Representation: An Informationally Complete Visualization of Mixed Quantum States
authors: Celina Bräutigam, Steffen J. Glaser, Dennis Huber
abstract: A deep understanding of quantum information theory is essential for quantum science and technology. However, quantum mechanics and particularly quantum information theory suffer from a lack of intuitive images. Visualization tools offer novel perspectives on many problems in quantum physics by revealing important properties of quantum states and processes that are otherwise obscured by abstract mathematical formalisms. Here, we extend the previously established BEADS representation of pure states to the so-called generalized BEADS representation of mixed quantum states. We introduce spherical functions, so-called beads to visualize correlation structures of mixed quantum states. A recursive optimization scheme is used to obtain minimum-entanglement pure state decompositions of all subsystems of a given N-qubit state. We show how correlation function components can be decomposed into individual contributions that directly correspond to different types of correlations of mixed states. This allows us to visually characterize the total correlation, genuine n-partite entanglement, nonclassical quantum-discord-type correlations as well as classical correlations. After outlining the mathematical details relevant for constructing the representation, we examine the generalized BEADS representations for various classes of mixed states including product, classically correlated, separable but nonclassically correlated, as well as entangled states. As exemplary applications of the generalized BEADS representation, we showcase entanglement distillation and the effects of noise channels.

infographic.key_insight: The paper extends BEADS from pure to mixed quantum states, giving an informationally complete visual language that separates total, classical, discord-like, and genuine multipartite quantum correlations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could help quantum hardware and algorithm teams diagnose state preparation, entanglement generation, and noise effects with more intuitive correlation visualizations.
method: Build a generalized BEADS representation for mixed N-qubit states using spherical “beads” to encode correlation structure.
Use a recursive optimization scheme to find minimum-entanglement pure-state decompositions for all subsystems.
Decompose correlation-function components into distinct contributions associated with classical, quantum-discord-type, and entanglement correlations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports qualitative case studies on product, classically correlated, separable but nonclassically correlated, and entangled states, plus examples in entanglement distillation and noisy channels.
infographic.watch_item: The recursive decomposition and visualization may be computationally expensive and its interpretations can depend on the chosen optimization and decomposition strategy.
infographic.paper_title: The Generalized BEADS Representation: An Informationally Complete Visualization of Mixed Quantum States

title: Gaussian entanglement and quantum communication: geodesic optimization and multimode bounds
authors: Hemant K. Mishra, Mark M. Wilde
abstract: Loss and noise limit the use of light to distribute entanglement, transmit quantum information, and establish secret keys. Gaussian states have a compact description in terms of means and covariance matrices, but their entanglement still requires global optimization. We develop a framework for computing Gaussian-restricted versions of the relative entropy of entanglement and Rains entanglement. An integral representation reveals a convex geometry under matrix geometric means and reduces Gaussian Rains entanglement to relative entropy minimized over Gaussian states with positive partial transpose. We obtain unique optimal reference states and additivity for independent Gaussian input states. Our convex-majorization algorithm has an explicit geometric convergence rate, uniform in the faithful regularization parameter and valid for pure input states. Controlled numerical integration and approximate convex subproblem solutions give a bit-complexity bound that is polynomial in accuracy bits for each fixed rational input covariance matrix, with explicit dependence on covariance size. These calculations bound extractable entanglement and, through the relative entropy of entanglement, extractable secret key. Teleportation simulation, energy allocation, and a convex optimization of passive-basis loss cores give bounds on quantum and private communication under an input-energy constraint, allowing arbitrary two-way classically assisted protocols. Two- and three-mode examples compare the bounds with achievable rates, including matching pure-loss benchmarks. Finally, we separate the Gaussian-restricted quantities from their unrestricted counterparts and give a photon-number truncation method with controlled error for computing the latter.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns Gaussian entanglement evaluation into a convex-geometric optimization problem, enabling efficient and provably convergent bounds on entanglement, secret key, and communication rates for lossy quantum channels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides practical performance limits and computable benchmarks for designing continuous-variable quantum communication systems under loss, noise, and energy constraints.
method: Derives Gaussian-restricted relative entropy and Rains entanglement via an integral representation over matrix geometric means.
Uses a convex-majorization algorithm with explicit geometric convergence and unique optimal Gaussian reference states.
Applies teleportation simulation, energy allocation, and passive-basis loss optimization to bound two-way assisted communication rates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports polynomial bit-complexity for fixed rational covariance inputs, explicit convergence rates, and two- and three-mode numerical examples that match known pure-loss benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest guarantees are for Gaussian-restricted quantities and fixed rational covariance matrices; unrestricted entanglement estimates require photon-number truncation with controlled but nontrivial approximation error.
infographic.paper_title: Gaussian entanglement and quantum communication: geodesic optimization and multimode bounds

title: Looking Beyond Visibility: Resolving the Temporal Structure of Continuous-Wave Four-Photon Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
authors: Sabine Häussler, Meritxell Cabrejo-Ponce, Ana Maria Torres, Baghdasar Baghdasaryan, Karen Lozano-Mendéz, Fabian Steinlechner
abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference underpins many photonic quantum information protocols and is commonly characterized by a single visibility parameter. This quantity is typically obtained by averaging over a fixed coincidence window, thereby discarding details of the underlying temporal structure that are critical in continuous-wave processes. Four-photon interference with continuous-wave sources furthermore requires photon pairs with long coherence times, which we generate in microring resonators and measure with ultrafast time-resolved detection. Here, we model and resolve their interference and temporal structure by recording all four photon arrival times and mapping their relative delays onto a three-dimensional coincidence histogram relative to a trigger detection. The resulting structure preserves relative arrival-time correlations that are usually discarded and enables post-processed optimization of coincidence windows to trade off visibility against count rate. This method provides a general benchmark for continuous-wave sources in interference-based quantum network protocols.

infographic.key_insight: By recording all four photon arrival times, the paper reveals and preserves the full temporal structure of continuous-wave four-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference instead of collapsing it into a single visibility number.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical benchmarking and optimization tool for photonic quantum network systems, letting engineers tune coincidence windows to balance interference visibility against usable count rate.
method: Generate long-coherence photon pairs in microring resonators under continuous-wave pumping
Use ultrafast time-resolved detection to record all four arrival times
Map relative delays into a 3D coincidence histogram referenced to a trigger detection
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports modeled and measured four-photon interference patterns with time-resolved 3D histograms, enabling post-processed coincidence-window optimization to trade off visibility versus count rate.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on ultrafast timing resolution and post-processing, so performance may depend strongly on detector jitter, timing calibration, and experimental stability.
infographic.paper_title: Looking Beyond Visibility: Resolving the Temporal Structure of Continuous-Wave Four-Photon Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference

title: Classification of quantum states through conserved operators
authors: Federico Petrovich, R. Rossignoli, M. Cerezo
abstract: Determining whether quantum states can be interconverted by a prescribed set of transformations is a fundamental problem in quantum information. Here we develop a general classification framework based on conserved operators (COs), i.e., not necessarily hermitian matrices having the state of interest as an eigenstate. We first show that COs belonging to the algebra generating the allowed transformations can be obtained from the kernel of a quantum covariance matrix. Their number determines the dimension of the accessible orbit, while their algebraic structure and eigenvalues provide further constraints on state convertibility. We establish general bounds on the number of COs and prove that highest-weight states, like separable states in the case of $n$ qudits, attain the maximum. We also show how these operators generate parent Hamiltonians having the characterized state as an exact ground state. We then also consider positive zero-eigenvalue COs, which encode forbidden directions of reduced density matrices and incorporate rank-based constraints into the same framework. Applying this approach to multiqubit SLOCC, we obtain complementary classifications from algebraic and rank COs. While for $n\leq 3$ qubits both lead to the usual classes, for $n=4$ qubits they distinguish 17 and 20 types separately, and 29 when combined. The combined classification yields 287 fixed types and $4$ continuous families for $n=5$ qubits, and 4926 fixed types and 147 continuous families for $n=6$ qubits, providing, to our knowledge, the most refined exhaustive classification of SLOCC-convertibility classes based on such data.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum states can be classified by conserved operators derived from transformation symmetries, revealing when states can or cannot be converted under a chosen dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework gives a systematic way to identify accessible state classes and exact parent Hamiltonians, which is useful for quantum control, simulation, and resource-state design.
method: Build conserved operators from the kernel of a quantum covariance matrix.
Use operator algebra and eigenvalue constraints to determine convertibility and orbit dimension.
Add positive zero-eigenvalue COs to capture rank-based restrictions in reduced density matrices.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports exhaustive multiqubit SLOCC classifications, distinguishing 29 types for 4 qubits and 4926 fixed types plus 147 continuous families for 6 qubits.
infographic.watch_item: The classification is highly expressive but may become computationally expensive and representation-dependent as system size and operator families grow.
infographic.paper_title: Classification of quantum states through conserved operators

title: Sparse-QITE: Discovering Compact Generators for Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution via Regularization Methods
authors: Rafael Gómez-Lurbe, Luca Ion, Alberto Acevedo, Andreu Anglés-Castillo
abstract: Quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE) provides a systematic route to ground-state preparation, but its cost grows rapidly with the locality $D$ of the unitary approximation, for which the local Pauli basis scales as $4^D$. We introduce Sparse-QITE, a regularized formulation that promotes compact generators, reducing the number of quantum operations and yielding circuits with fewer gates and lower depth. We derive rigorous bounds on the sparsification error and benchmark the method in one-dimensional transverse-field Ising and antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models. Sparse-QITE exhibits a controllable sparsity--accuracy trade-off while retaining strong compression even in the high-accuracy regime. In scalability experiments with respect to $D$, the active support grows much more slowly than in standard QITE and, in several regimes, approximately saturates over the domain sizes studied. After circuit construction and transpilation, some of the largest-domain cases require only about $1\%$ of the standard-QITE gate count while maintaining high accuracy. We further introduce adaptive and active-discovery variants: the former selects the regularization strength dynamically during the evolution, while the latter reduces the number of Pauli expectation values that need to be evaluated and, consequently, the measurement requirements. These results establish sparsity-promoting regularization as a route toward more resource-efficient QITE. More broadly, these results suggest that sparsity-promoting regularization may also benefit variational quantum algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse-QITE uses regularization to discover compact QITE generators, cutting circuit depth and gate count while preserving high ground-state accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a practical path to lower-resource quantum simulation by reducing both gate execution cost and measurement overhead in QITE workflows.
method: Add sparsity-promoting regularization to the local Pauli generator fit.
Select a compact subset of Pauli terms to approximate imaginary-time updates.
Use adaptive regularization and active discovery to further reduce measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks on 1D transverse-field Ising and antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models show a controllable sparsity–accuracy trade-off, with some large-domain cases using about 1% of the standard-QITE gate count after transpilation.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on regularization tuning and problem structure, so overly aggressive sparsification could reduce accuracy or limit transferability across models.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse-QITE: Discovering Compact Generators for Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution via Regularization Methods
